versions.title: A Day at Fertile GroundWorks
versions.summary: Yesterday, I had the opportunity to volunteer at Fertile GroundWorks with some friends. It was a great experience to give back to the community and learn more about sustainable gardening. The garden grows fresh produce that helps support lo…
versions.text: Yesterday, I had the opportunity to volunteer at Fertile GroundWorks with some friends. It was a great experience to give back to the community and learn more about sustainable gardening. The garden grows fresh produce that helps support local organizations like Tri-Valley Haven to provide food for people in need. I loved seeing how faith can be put into action through caring for the community and serving others. No photos this time, but plenty of good memories! Grateful for the experience and looking forward to more opportunities to give back!

versions.title: Why I built duskline
versions.summary: I wanted to check the weather in Tokyo as easily as I check it at home, on my phone or my computer.
versions.text: I wanted to be able to open the same weather app on whatever screen I had nearby. On my phone I might only want to know if I should take a jacket. At a desk I might spend longer looking through the hourly chart. Both should feel like a full version of the app. That’s why I built duskline for the web. A forecast beyond my own city I wanted to look up the weather far from home, too. Open-Meteo gives duskline broad forecast coverage. It serves forecasts by coordinates and draws on regional models where available, with global models covering other areas. I can look up Tokyo or Cape Town from the same screen I use for the Bay Area. Put those forecasts side by side and a plain word like “Today” starts to get tricky. At four in the afternoon in the Bay Area, it’s already tomorrow in Tokyo. The app has to know which day each city is on before it can draw a useful hourly chart. Which time zone is it? A weather provider can send an hourly forecast labeled 18:00 in the city’s local time. The clock reading is easy to display. The tricky bit comes when the app needs to put it on a timeline. If the browser treats a timestamp with no offset as the device’s local time, Tokyo’s six in the evening lands at six in the evening in California. In duskline, the city’s time zone comes along with the forecast. I use it to interpret those clock readings and to decide which day is “today.” I can then put the current time and the forecast hours on the same chart, while keeping the labels in the time the city actually uses. Temperature map of North America in duskline, with Las Vegas selected and a forecast slider labeled 10:00 AM UTC and 2:00 AM PST. On the weather map, the forecast slider shows the selected hour in both UTC and local time. How duskline draws the sky The sky in a city’s detail view comes from a similar idea. A clear night and a clear afternoon might both read “Clear,” but they don’t feel anything alike. The city’s local light and conditions shape the colors. Clouds and rain can give the view a different character before I read the forecast. There’s a limit to how much I want that background to do. If I’m trying to decide when to go out, I need to see when the chance of rain picks up. I kept that in the hourly chart, where I can move across the day and read the values. The sky gives me a first impression, and the chart lets me check it. Sydney’s forecast against a bright blue sky with a low sun, with local hourly and ten-day outlooks below. Sydney in the afternoon, with showers in the hourly outlook. San Francisco’s forecast against a dark sky with a moon, with the hourly outlook continuing past midnight. San Francisco after dark, with the hourly forecast rolling past midnight. When there’s an official alert San Francisco’s screenshot shows a clear night and a coastal flood advisory on the same screen. Both can be true. The forecast describes the sky and the next few hours, while the advisory is about a hazard along the coast. That’s why I put public alerts above the hourly forecast. You can open an alert to see details like the areas it covers, when it ends, and who issued it. For eligible U.S. locations, duskline fetches active alerts from the National Weather Service . Where an official feed is available internationally, it uses the IFRC Alert Hub . The Sydney screenshot shows an example from Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, which issued a strong wind warning for specific coastal waters. Checking the forecast offline I wanted duskline to be as easy to reach as any other weather app. I made it an installable web app (a PWA), so it can sit on my phone’s Home Screen and open in its own window on a computer. The same forecast I can glance at on my phone is there when I want to sit down and look more closely. Say I check the weather before heading out, then lose my signal on the way. I can reopen duskline and read the recent forecast it saved on that device, along with the time it was last checked. If I checked it an hour ago, I can still look up when the rain was expected. If I checked it yesterday, I know to refresh when I get a signal. Fresh forecasts and public alerts need a connection. Look at two skies Open duskline , find your city and one several time zones away, and check the local time in each. Then look at the hourly forecast in both. What does the next hour look like there? That’s my favorite question to ask of Horizon , especially when it’s getting dark outside my own window.

versions.title: A workbench in the browser
versions.summary: Why I built Kit, an ad-free collection of browser tools for jobs like shrinking a photo or finding a symbol.
versions.text: I wanted one place for the little jobs I do in my browser. Some days that’s shrinking a photo or putting a few pages into a PDF. Other times I just need to find the right symbol and paste it into something I’m writing. I had privacy concerns about sending files to an online utility for a five-second edit, and I didn’t want ads in the way. So I built Kit around a simple idea. Open one tab, do the job, and get back to what you were doing. Four colored curves in Kit’s function grapher, with their values marked at the same x coordinate. Kit’s function grapher lets me trace several curves at once and compare their values. What makes a photo smaller? “Make it smaller” can mean two different things. A 4,000-pixel-wide photo can become 1,600 pixels wide. That gives the browser fewer pixels to store. Or I can keep the same dimensions and ask JPEG to use less detail when it writes those pixels out. Both can save space, but they give up different things. The first is often enough for a photo that will only ever be seen in a chat window. The second is worth a closer look if there’s small text or fine detail I want to keep. In Kit, the browser decodes the original, draws it at the new size on a canvas, and encodes a fresh file. The original stays where it was. I put the before and after file sizes next to the result because a quality slider is a poor answer to “will this fit?” The size of the actual output is the answer. One less trip through Downloads The part I like most comes after the first edit. If the photo needs to go into a PDF, I can send the result straight to Images → PDF . The next tool receives the image in memory. I only need to save the file I came for. A folder full of nearly identical intermediate copies is a surprisingly easy thing to build by accident. That’s also where Kit’s privacy promise becomes concrete. The site serves the tools, and the browser does the file work on the device. For a photo or PDF, I like that opening a web page and handing a server my file can be two separate things. The tools I kept looking for Some jobs are so small they’re easy to leave out of a toolkit. The Symbol browser came from one of those. I wanted a place to look up a character when I knew what it meant but couldn’t type it. Try searching for “right arrow” or U+2192 . Either way, you can copy → as text and carry on writing. That felt as worth building as a tool with a progress bar. Kit’s Symbol browser in a desktop window, with the right arrow selected and a Copied confirmation above the grid. The right arrow from the example, ready to paste as text. A toolbox I can take offline I also wanted Kit to feel like something I could keep. It’s an installable web app (a PWA), so I can open it from my phone’s Home Screen or in its own window on a computer. If I know I’ll be without Wi-Fi, I can use Settings → Offline access to download the tools and languages I want. Kit checks the saved files and shows which tools are ready. That lets me keep a small kit on each device. A photo compressor and the Symbol browser might be enough on my phone. I can also save the larger PDF, audio, and video engines if I need them. Once the tools I’ve chosen are ready, I can open them and do the file work with the connection off. Try it with a photo Open Compress images and pick a JPEG. Set the maximum width to 1,600 pixels, then compare the result with the original. Run it again at the same width with a lower quality setting. Zoom in on a place with small text, leaves, or hair and see where you start to notice a difference. The useful number is the smallest file you’d still be happy to send.

versions.title: That “noise” was data
versions.summary: Exploring SAME through Signal Lab: What message is encoded in an emergency alert
versions.text: At first, the three bursts at the beginning of an emergency alert just sounded like noise to me. Then I found out they were carrying information. That made them much more interesting. Before anyone starts speaking, a receiver can already have information about the event, the affected area, and the message’s valid period. I wanted to look inside that exchange, so I built a SAME study mode into Signal Lab . Our Special Guest: S.A.M.E. SAME stands for Specific Area Message Encoding . It is used by NOAA Weather Radio and the U.S. Emergency Alert System (EAS). The opening bursts carry a machine-readable header; the spoken announcement is a separate part of the message. NOAA explains how receivers use those fields to select relevant alerts. The three bursts are repeated transmissions, rather than three different pitches. Within each burst, two frequencies carry the data: 1,562.5 Hz for a 0 and about 2,083.3 Hz for a 1, at roughly 520.83 bits per second. The longer attention signal is a separate sound. The EAS protocol specifies that distinction. Once decoded, the header becomes a compact line of text. The example below describes a fictional weekly test for Los Angeles County. Try changing its event, area, or valid period, then select a field to read it more closely.  The small details matter The location field is worth slowing down for. 006037 splits into 0 · 06 · 037 : partition, California, Los Angeles County. It is not a ZIP code. The first digit can select a locally defined part of a county; changing it does not automatically create a meaningful area. NOAA’s partition guide describes the distinction. The time field has its own compactness: 3021800 means day 302 of the year at 18:00 UTC. It does not carry the year. The sender field has a fixed width, so even the two spaces after SIGLAB in this example are doing a job. Before the readable header, a sixteen-byte preamble helps the receiver synchronize. NOAA’s archived technical specification documents the byte format and timing. What I built in Signal Lab In Signal Lab, SAME sits alongside a small audio modem and Morse-code tools. The project brings encoding, decoding, and explanations into one place so I can change something and see what happens to the signal. SAME is one part of that wider experiment. The SAME mode lets me edit header fields, look up geographic codes, generate the corresponding waveform, and feed it directly into the decoder with Test in decoder . That internal test is silent: it checks generated samples without sending them through a speaker or microphone. The receiver also tracks the repeated headers. One implementation detail is easy to overlook: a decoder can detect the same physical burst through several timing candidates. Counting each detection as another transmission would make a single burst look like several copies. Signal Lab uses the positions of those detections in the audio to avoid counting them twice. Its comparison is deliberately limited to complete, parsed headers. Three matching bursts satisfy the app’s comparison; missing bursts leave an incomplete set, and different headers produce a conflict. It does not reconstruct damaged headers through bit-by-bit majority voting, and matching copies do not establish a sender’s identity. The experiment above models that comparison, rather than every rule used by operational equipment. From a sound to something readable This is the part I wanted to share: a sound I had dismissed as noise had a structure I could inspect. The fields, timing, and repetitions each contribute something specific. Building a small tool around them gave me a way to follow the information all the way from a header to a waveform and back. Continue in Signal Lab → Learn → EAS / SAME for the annotated format, or open Encoder → EAS / SAME in the project to try the full tool. Signal Lab is an educational project, not certified alert equipment. This article’s experiment is silent. U.S. restrictions cover EAS codes and attention signals, including recordings and simulations; a test label does not authorize their transmission. See 47 CFR § 11.45 before considering playback or distribution.

versions.title: 原来，“噪声” 里藏着数据
versions.summary: 用 Signal Lab 探索 SAME 编码：紧急警报里的报头藏着什么信息？
versions.text: 最开始，我认为紧急警报开头的那三段声音只是噪声，吸引人的注意。后来才发现，里面竟然包含很多信息。 这一下就有意思了起来：在 “开始说话” 前，接收设备就可能已经知道发生了哪类事件、涉及哪些区域，以及消息的有效时长。我想探究这个过程到底如何实现，于是把 SAME 学习功能做进了 Signal Lab 。 一段神秘的报头 SAME 的全称是 Specific Area Message Encoding ，用于 NOAA 气象广播和美国的紧急警报系统 EAS。开头的短促信号传输的是供机器读取的报头，语音播报则是消息的另一个部分。 NOAA 的说明 介绍了接收设备如何利用这些字段筛选与自己有关的警报。 这里的 “三段” 指重复发送三次。每段信号内部用两种频率传递数据：1,562.5 Hz 表示 0，约 2,083.3 Hz 表示 1，速率约为每秒 520.83 位。后面那段较长的提示音是另一回事。 EAS 协议 分别规定了它们的格式。 解码之后，我们会发现报头其实是一行文字。下面用一个虚构的洛杉矶县每周测试消息做例子。可以试着更改一些数据，再看看里面的含义。  一些值得细看的地方 地理区域码就很有意思。 006037 可以拆成 0 · 06 · 037 ，分别对应分区、加利福尼亚州和洛杉矶县。它不是邮政编码。第一位可以选择由当地定义的县内分区，随便改一个数字，并不代表就选中了一个实际有效的区域。 NOAA 的分区说明 解释了这一点。 时间字段也很紧凑： 3021800 表示一年中的第 302 天、UTC 18:00，但它本身不包含年份。发送方标识有固定长度，所以本例中 SIGLAB 后面的两个空格也有作用。在这些可读字符之前，还有十六字节的前导码帮助接收端同步。 NOAA 存档的技术规范 记录了字节格式和时序。 我在 Signal Lab 里做了什么 在 Signal Lab 里，SAME 与音频调制解调器和摩尔斯电码工具放在一起。我把编码、解码和相关说明集中在一个地方，方便改动参数，再看看信号发生了什么变化。SAME 是这个声音与数据实验的一部分。 在 SAME 模式中，我可以修改报头字段、查找地理区域码、生成对应的波形，再通过 Test in decoder（在解码器中测试） 直接送入解码器。这个内部测试是无声的：它处理生成的采样数据，不经过扬声器和麦克风。 接收端还会追踪重复发送的报头。其中有个容易忽略的实现细节：解码器可能通过几个不同的时序候选检测到同一次物理发送。如果把每次检测都算作一次新发送，一段信号就可能被误计成多份副本。Signal Lab 根据这些检测在音频中的位置，避免重复计数。 目前它比较的是完整、已经解析出来的报头。三次一致，才满足应用里的比较条件；少收到是不完整，不同则标记为冲突。它不会用逐位多数表决来重建损坏的报头，而且即使副本一致也不能证明发送方的身份。上面的实验演示的是这个比较过程，而不是实际警报设备的全部处理规则。 从一段声音，到可以解码的数据 这就是我想分享的小发现：原本被我当作噪声的声音，里面有可以拆开研究的结构。字符、时长和反复播放，各有具体作用。把它们做成一个小工具，也让我能顺着信息走一遍：从数据到波形，再从波形读回数据。 可以在 Signal Lab → Learn（学习）→ EAS / SAME 阅读带注释的格式说明，再打开项目中的 Encoder（编码器）→ EAS / SAME，试试完整工具。 Signal Lab 是学习项目，不是经过认证的警报设备。本文的实验不播放声音。美国对 EAS 编码和提示音的传输有限制，也包括录音和模拟信号；标注“测试”并不等于获得授权。考虑播放或分发之前，请先阅读 47 CFR § 11.45 。
